_comment: SKILL BLUEPRINT — output of the Spec agent, input to the Generator agent.
subject: math
description: Students use triangle congruence criteria ($\text{SSS}$, $\text{SAS}$, $\text{ASA}$, $\text{AAS}$, $\text{HL}$) and triangle similarity criteria ($\text{AA}$, $\text{SAS}\sim$, $\text{SSS}\sim$) to solve numerical and geometric problems and to justify relationships in figures. They identify when two triangles are congruent or similar, set up and solve proportions from corresponding sides of similar triangles, find missing side lengths and angle measures, apply the relationship that congruent triangles have corresponding parts congruent ($\text{CPCTC}$) and similar triangles have proportional corresponding sides, and write short justifications for why a relationship (e.g. parallel segments, midsegments, equal ratios) must hold.
subSkills: State the correct congruence criterion ($\text{SSS}$, $\text{SAS}$, $\text{ASA}$, $\text{AAS}$, $\text{HL}$) that proves two triangles congruent from given marks
State the correct similarity criterion ($\text{AA}$, $\text{SAS}\sim$, $\text{SSS}\sim$) that proves two triangles similar
Write a correct correspondence between vertices of two congruent or similar triangles
Set up a proportion from corresponding sides of similar triangles and solve for a missing length
Use the scale factor (ratio of similarity) to find a missing side, perimeter, or to relate areas by the square of the scale factor
Apply $\text{CPCTC}$ to conclude that a remaining pair of sides or angles is congruent once triangles are proven congruent
Use shared sides, vertical angles, the Reflexive Property, and parallel-line angle relationships to supply the needed congruent/proportional parts
Solve overlapping-triangle and nested-triangle problems (e.g. a triangle cut by a line parallel to one side) using the Side-Splitter relationship
Write a short logical justification (statement + reason) for why a relationship holds

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the congruence criterion
problemArchetypes.example: In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$, $AB = DE$, $\angle A = \angle D$, and $AC = DF$. Which criterion proves $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$? Answer: $\text{SAS}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the similarity criterion
problemArchetypes.example: Two triangles have $\angle A = \angle X = 52^\circ$ and $\angle B = \angle Y = 71^\circ$. Which criterion proves $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle XYZ$? Answer: $\text{AA}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Solve a proportion for a missing side
problemArchetypes.example: $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ with $AB = 6$, $DE = 9$, and $BC = 8$. Find $EF$. Set up $\frac{6}{9} = \frac{8}{EF}$ so $EF = 12$.

problemArchetypes.name: Scale factor with perimeter or area
problemArchetypes.example: $\triangle PQR \sim \triangle STU$ with scale factor $\frac{2}{3}$. If the area of $\triangle PQR$ is $12$, find the area of $\triangle STU$. Answer: $12 \cdot \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2 = 27$.

problemArchetypes.name: Side-Splitter / parallel line within a triangle
problemArchetypes.example: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ on $\overline{AB}$ and $E$ on $\overline{AC}$ with $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}$. If $AD = 4$, $DB = 6$, and $AE = 5$, find $EC$. Set up $\frac{4}{6} = \frac{5}{EC}$ so $EC = \frac{15}{2}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Overlapping or shared-side triangles with CPCTC
problemArchetypes.example: Given $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{CB}$ and $\overline{BD}$ bisects $\angle ABC$, prove $\overline{AD} \cong \overline{CD}$. Triangles share $\overline{BD}$, so $\triangle ABD \cong \triangle CBD$ by $\text{SAS}$, and $\overline{AD} \cong \overline{CD}$ by $\text{CPCTC}$.

problemArchetypes.name: Indirect measurement (real-world similar triangles)
problemArchetypes.example: A $6$ ft person casts a $4$ ft shadow while a flagpole casts a $26$ ft shadow at the same time. Find the height of the flagpole. Set up $\frac{6}{4} = \frac{h}{26}$ so $h = 39$ ft.

problemArchetypes.name: Solve for a variable in side expressions
problemArchetypes.example: $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$ with $AB = 2x$, $DE = 10$, $BC = x + 3$, $EF = 8$. Find $x$. Set up $\frac{2x}{10} = \frac{x+3}{8}$, cross multiply $16x = 10x + 30$, so $x = 5$.

Easy.description: Single-step recognition or one proportion. The criterion or correspondence is given or directly visible, and at most one proportion is solved with small whole-number answers. A diagram or all needed measures are stated.
constraints: Name the congruence/similarity criterion from explicitly given congruent/proportional parts, OR solve one proportion $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{x}$ for $x$
All four relevant measures are whole numbers $\le 24$ and the answer is a whole number or a simple fraction
Correspondence between triangles is given in the similarity/congruence statement (e.g. $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF$)
No shared sides, overlapping triangles, or auxiliary reasoning required

Medium.description: Two steps: establish the correspondence or criterion, then compute. Includes scale-factor reasoning, side-splitter (parallel line) setups, solving a linear equation that arises from a single proportion, or applying CPCTC after a one-line congruence argument.
constraints: Student must determine the correct correspondence or select the right criterion before computing
May require a side-splitter proportion, a perimeter via scale factor, or solving $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{x}$ where the answer is a non-integer fraction
May involve one variable in a single side expression solved by cross multiplication
Uses vertical angles, a shared side (Reflexive), or parallel-line angles to supply one missing congruent/proportional part

Hard.description: Multi-step problems combining several relationships: prove similarity/congruence then use it to find a length, area ratio as the square of the scale factor, overlapping or nested triangles, or a short multi-statement justification. Requires reading a figure or context, choosing the criterion, and chaining two or more computations.
constraints: Requires proving the triangles related (criterion + reason) AND then solving for a missing quantity
May use the area ratio $= (\text{scale factor})^2$, nested/overlapping triangles, or two linked proportions
May require a 3-to-4 statement justification (statement and reason) for the relationship
Variable may appear in two expressions or the answer may be an exact radical or fraction

difficultyRubric._split: If authored as two worksheets: tier1 covers Easy to Medium (recognizing criteria, single proportions, scale factor, basic side-splitter, simple CPCTC); tier2 covers Medium to Hard (variable-in-expression proportions, area ratios, overlapping/nested triangles, multi-statement justifications, indirect measurement). The single ramped worksheet runs Easy items 1 to 5, Medium items 6 to 11, Hard items 12 to 15.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats $\text{AAA}$ or $\text{SSA}$ as a congruence criterion
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects $\text{AAA}$ to 'prove congruence' (it only proves similarity) or selects $\text{SSA}$ as a valid congruence criterion

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student matches corresponding sides incorrectly, pairing non-corresponding parts
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Sets up $\frac{AB}{EF}$ instead of $\frac{AB}{DE}$, e.g. computes $EF = \frac{6 \cdot 8}{9}$ from a mismatched pairing

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student inverts the proportion, putting the ratio upside down
Student scales area by the scale factor instead of its square
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Multiplies the area by $\frac{3}{2}$ to get $18$ instead of by $\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2$ to get $27$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student adds the scale factor to each side instead of multiplying
commonMisconceptions.distractor: From a scale factor making sides $3$ longer additively, gets $EF = 8 + 3 = 11$ instead of $EF = 8 \cdot \frac{9}{6} = 12$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student misapplies the Side-Splitter ratio, comparing a part to the whole inconsistently
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Sets up $\frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{AE}{EC}$ (part-to-whole equals part-to-part) instead of $\frac{AD}{DB} = \frac{AE}{EC}$, e.g. getting $EC = \frac{25}{2}$ instead of $\frac{15}{2}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student concludes congruence from similarity, treating similar triangles as having equal side lengths
commonMisconceptions.distractor: States the missing side equals its corresponding side ($EF = 8$) because the triangles are 'similar,' ignoring the scale factor

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student cites $\text{CPCTC}$ before the triangles are proven congruent (circular reasoning)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a justification that uses $\text{CPCTC}$ as the reason for the very congruence it is meant to prove, rather than as a conclusion after congruence is established
